new_groups.label: Burr's conspiracy and trial
new_groups.definition: Documents and reports of Aaron Burr's alleged conspiracy and his trial, as the 1807 papers printed them: the President's message to Congress of 22 January, a New York report of news from New Orleans (February), Chief Justice Marshall's opinion on committing Burr (April), the jury's verdict in the treason trial (September), and Marshall's opinion of 20 October after the trial. Contains those five groups; the wider coverage is not included. The message and the reports carry allegations; the jury found the charge of treason not proved.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message on the conspiracy
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of 22 January 1807, sent at the request of the House, on 'an illegal combination of private individuals' against the peace of the Union and a military expedition planned against Spanish territory, with the measures taken to suppress it. It names Aaron Burr as the principal actor. Its enclosures (General Wilkinson's affidavit and letters) are not counted separately.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: News from New Orleans: 'Burr in arms'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a New York report (3 February 1807) of news from New Orleans brought by the brig Neptune: General Wilkinson had refused Burr passage, the city was under arms, and Burr was said to be at Natchez with 600 men and an advanced guard of 200 cavalry. The numbers are a report, not an observed fact.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Marshall's opinion on committing Burr
new_groups.definition: Printings of Chief Justice Marshall's opinion of 1 April 1807 at Richmond on the motion to commit Aaron Burr on two charges: he committed him for setting on foot an expedition against Spanish territory, a misdemeanor, but not for treason, finding no proof yet that war had been levied. Includes one printing of a summary of the opinion.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The verdict: 'not proved to be guilty'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the jury's written verdict in Aaron Burr's trial for treason at Richmond on 1 September 1807, 'We of the jury find that Aaron Burr is not proved to be guilty under this indictment by any evidence submitted to us. We therefore find him not guilty', quoted in accounts of that day's proceedings, with Burr's objection to its form. Three different accounts carry it; most papers printed the same one.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Marshall's opinion of 20 October
new_groups.definition: Printings of Chief Justice Marshall's opinion of 20 October 1807 at Richmond, after the treason trial, on the motion to commit Burr, Blennerhassett and Israel Smith to be tried elsewhere for treason and misdemeanor: he held it improper to commit them on the charge of treason, and committed Burr and Blennerhassett for preparing and providing the means for a military expedition. Includes printings of a Richmond report that quotes the opinion's conclusion.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Monroe and Pinkney: a treaty agreed
new_groups.definition: Printings of the letter of James Monroe and William Pinkney from London, 27 December 1806, to the Secretary of State: they had agreed with the British commissioners to conclude a treaty on all the points of their negotiation, on terms they trusted the government would approve. The President sent it to Congress on 19 February 1807. Several papers printed it again in October and November, after the treaty had been set aside.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Lübeck stormed
new_groups.definition: Printings of a report from Lübeck (9 or 10 November 1806) of the French attack of 6 November, which took the town from the Prussians: 'the most dreadful day in the annals of Lubeck'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Sir Harford Jones on the Russian army
new_groups.definition: Printings of a London paragraph of January 1807: Sir Harford Jones, back from the Russian headquarters, had never seen an army in a higher state of discipline or more eager to meet the enemy, with news of the Russian columns and of the French crossing the Vistula. It is one witness's account. Two versions circulated, dated London 6 January and 'From the Liverpool Advertiser'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Bennigsen's account of Pultusk
new_groups.definition: Printings of General Bennigsen's report to the King of Prussia on the battle of Pultusk (26 December 1806), the Russian official account, in which he writes that he repulsed the French attack on every point.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The French army's 66th bulletin
new_groups.definition: Printings of the 66th bulletin of the French Grand Army (Osterode, 14 March 1807): the army rests in cantonments, with skirmishes between the outposts. New York papers had it by the brig Alonzo from Bordeaux, with the 65th.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The 78th bulletin: the action of Spanden
new_groups.definition: Printings of an abstract of the 78th bulletin of the French Grand Army (Heilsberg, 12 June 1807), received at Boston from Nantes: the overtures of peace made in the winter, broken off by the Russian attacks, and the action of Spanden on 5 June.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Armistice between France and Russia
new_groups.definition: Printings of the armistice between the French and Russian armies agreed at Tilsit on 21 June 1807 (signed by Berthier and Prince Labanoff), the preliminary to the peace.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Driver at Charleston
new_groups.definition: Reports of the British sloop of war Driver, which the President had barred from American ports, anchoring in Charleston harbour in April and May 1807: the commandant of Fort Johnson's demand that she leave, and her commander's answer. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Fort Johnson orders the Driver out
new_groups.definition: Printings of the letter of Captain Michael Kalteisen, commandant of Fort Johnson in Charleston harbour (2 May 1807), to the commander of the British sloop of war Driver, which a proclamation of the President had barred from American harbours: she must leave within twenty-four hours. Most papers printed it inside a Charleston report of the Driver's arrival, reprinted from New York; the papers give the proclamation different dates.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Driver's commander answers
new_groups.definition: Printings of the answer of Captain William Love, commanding the British sloop of war Driver (Rebellion Roads, Charleston, 3 May 1807), to Captain Kalteisen: he doubted the authority by which the demand was written, knew nothing of a proclamation of May 1807, and would not leave until ready.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Chesapeake affair
new_groups.definition: Documents and reports of the attack of the British ship Leopard on the American frigate Chesapeake off the Virginia capes on 22 June 1807, and its aftermath, as the 1807 papers printed them: the National Intelligencer's account, the President's proclamation of 2 July, Admiral Berkeley's order, the opinion of the court of inquiry on Commodore Barron, and the House committee's report. Contains those five groups; the wider coverage is not included.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The National Intelligencer's account of the attack
new_groups.definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's account of 26 June 1807, headed 'British Outrage': the Leopard, one of the British squadron at the capes, followed the Chesapeake out to sea, demanded three men said to be deserters, and fired on her until she struck.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's proclamation of 2 July
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's proclamation of 2 July 1807, which recited the attack on the Chesapeake and required all armed vessels bearing commissions under the British government to leave the harbours and waters of the United States, forbidding all intercourse with them.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Admiral Berkeley's order
new_groups.definition: Printings of the order of Vice-Admiral George Cranfield Berkeley, British commander in chief at Halifax (1 June 1807), directing the captains under his command, if they met the Chesapeake at sea, to show her captain the order and search her for the deserters named in its margin. American papers printed it from late July.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The court of inquiry on the Chesapeake
new_groups.definition: Printings of the opinion of the naval court of inquiry held on board the Chesapeake at Norfolk (5 October to 4 November 1807) on the conduct of Commodore James Barron: among other findings, that the Chesapeake was prematurely surrendered when she was nearly prepared for battle. Includes one printing of its conclusion only.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The House committee's report
new_groups.definition: Printings of a summary of the report made to the House on 17 November 1807 by Mr. Blount for the committee on the part of the President's message relating to aggressions, with the report's conclusion quoted: the outrage on the Chesapeake 'has been stamped with circumstances of indignity and insult' with scarcely a parallel.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Commodore Douglas and the Mayor of Norfolk
new_groups.definition: The letters exchanged in July 1807 between Commodore John E. Douglas, commanding the British squadron in Hampton Roads, and Richard E. Lee, Mayor of Norfolk, over the Norfolk committee's ban on communication with the British ships, with the report of Littleton W. Tazewell, who carried the Mayor's answer. Contains those four groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Commodore Douglas's letter of 3 July
new_groups.definition: Printings of Commodore Douglas's letter to the Mayor of Norfolk (Bellona, Hampton Roads, 3 July 1807): unless the committee's resolution forbidding communication with the British consul and ships was annulled, he would stop every vessel bound in or out of Norfolk; it rested with the inhabitants 'either to engage in a war or remain on terms of peace'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Mayor's answer of 4 July
new_groups.definition: Printings of the answer of Richard E. Lee, Mayor of Norfolk, to Commodore Douglas (4 July 1807): 'the American people are not to be intimidated by menace'; the ban was an act of individuals, not of the government, and the inhabitants would protect themselves against any aggression.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Tazewell's report to the Mayor
new_groups.definition: Printings of the report of Littleton W. Tazewell to the Mayor of Norfolk (5 July 1807) on delivering the Mayor's answer on board the Bellona: Douglas said his letter had been misapprehended and that he intended no menace. Includes one shorter account of the report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Commodore Douglas's letter of 6 July
new_groups.definition: Printings of Commodore Douglas's second letter to the Mayor of Norfolk (Bellona, Hampton Roads, 6 July 1807): every circumstance had been discussed with the gentlemen who carried the Mayor's answer, and he would use every exertion, consistent with the honour of the British flag, toward an amicable end.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Congress called early, 1807
new_groups.definition: The President's proclamation of 30 July 1807 calling Congress to meet on 26 October instead of in December, and his message to the session on 27 October. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The proclamation calling Congress
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's proclamation of 30 July 1807 that 'great and weighty matters' required Congress to meet at Washington on Monday 26 October. The National Intelligencer printed it seven times, as a standing notice.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message of 27 October
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress at the opening of the special session, 27 October 1807: the British answer on the treaty, the attack on the Chesapeake and the proclamation that followed, the defence of the ports, the Burr trials, the finances, and the Indian nations.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: London: 'the question of peace or war'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a London paragraph of October 1807: the British ministers had delivered to Monroe and Pinkney their final answer on the leading points in dispute, so that 'the question of peace or war with America' was decided as far as it could be in England, and Monroe was preparing to leave. It is a London paper's report and forecast.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: An Antwerp letter: ships to or from England to be taken
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a house in Antwerp to one in Bordeaux (28 September 1807), brought by the Sally-Barker-Windsor: 'We understand' that the Emperor had ordered every vessel bound to or from England to be captured, 'a mortal blow to the American commerce'. It reports a rumoured order.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families of 1807 that reach 4 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running), were split into single printed items (items.json: 177 items in 7 or more papers, 31 in 9 or more). Those items were read and the stories chosen by the rule below. Each chosen item's printings were looked for with phrase searches over all 4,167 pages of 1807 in both transcriptions (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json), and every hit was read. Papers with pages in a story's weeks but no printing were searched by hand with loose keywords. Every admitted printing was then checked against its page scan (SCAN_PROTOCOL.md, scan_points.json); 39 crops were placed by hand where the text-layer locator missed the passage.
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: As for 1776: every single item printed in 9 or more newspapers was admitted, except digests of unrelated paragraphs and items that need careful framing. Items in 7 or 8 papers were chosen to cover the months and the main kinds of news. Stories are counted item by item; where one publication holds several documents (the Norfolk letters of July, the Chesapeake papers, the Burr affair), each document is its own group under a parent story. Every group reaches 7 or more papers. A paper that printed an item again later counts each printing.
added_by_phrase_search: BJ 1807-04-24 p2: a summary of Marshall's opinion of 1 April in a Richmond report (condensed report), found by the hand search
WR 1807-07-30 p2: a shorter, third-person account of Tazewell's report (condensed report)
LS 1807-09-10 p3: the verdict in the account most papers printed, on a torn page whose transcription keeps only fragments, found by the hand search

counted_item_by_item.Laws printed by authority: The acts repealing the salt duties, continuing the suspension of trade with parts of St. Domingo, on Virginia military warrants and prohibiting the importation of slaves were each counted in 9 or 10 papers because their titles also stand in the List of Acts and in reports of debates; by their enacting text they reach 3 to 7 papers.
counted_item_by_item.The President's message of 22 January: The message and its enclosures (Wilkinson's affidavit, letters of Burr and Bollman) are one publication, counted once by the message's opening.
counted_item_by_item.The Norfolk letters of July: Four documents printed together (Douglas's letter, the Mayor's answer, Tazewell's report, Douglas's second letter), each its own group under a parent story.
counted_item_by_item.The Burr verdict: Quoted in three different accounts of the court's proceedings; the group is the verdict as quoted (quoted_document).

not_admitted.The List of Acts passed during the secon: An index of unrelated laws, treated like a digest.
not_admitted.Other laws printed by authority: By their enacting text in fewer than 9 papers: the salt duties (5), Virginia military warrants (7; a weekly legal notice in the Virginia Argus), the suspension of the non-importation act (1). The proclamation suspending that act further (7 papers) was not chosen.
not_admitted.News digests: Runs of London and continental paragraphs printed in pieces (the London news by the Manchester packet, the Hamburg and Berlin paragraphs of January). Single paragraphs that reach 9 papers are admitted (Harford Jones).
not_admitted.Other Burr items: The President's messages of 28 January and 10 February (3 papers or fewer by their openings); reports that Burr was bailed at Natchez (4); a Richmond report of his examination that misstates the outcome (PGz, NHG, April); a NHG commentary of 6 October quoting the verdict.
not_admitted.The President's message of 19 February w: Counted under Monroe and Pinkney's letter where the letter is printed, not otherwise.
not_admitted.The court of inquiry's opening days (5 p: A different item from the court's opinion.
not_admitted.Candidates in 7 or 8 papers not chosen i: The House committee's second report on aggressions (8); the proclamation pardoning army deserters (7); the War Department's circular on volunteer companies (7); the Norfolk and Portsmouth resolutions of 24 June (7); a London report of peace between England, Russia and Turkey (7); the articles of the peace of Tilsit (7); the report that Britain disclaims searching ships of war (7); Bennigsen's dispatch of 10 February (7).
not_admitted.The Embargo: The President's message of 18 December (4 papers) and the Embargo Act of 22 December (5 papers by 31 December); most printings fall in January 1808.

for_user_decision.The act to prohibit the importation of s: Printed in full by authority in NI, a VA extra, HUS, NHG and an EN extra; its title in the List of Acts (10 papers) and in House debates on amending it.
for_user_decision.News from the Republic of Hayti (Baltimo: Christophe's attack on Port-au-Prince and a republican constitution; ADA also printed the constitution. The act on trade with parts of St. Domingo is in 3 papers.
for_user_decision.Robert MacDonald's death and funeral (No: A named seaman wounded on the Chesapeake; Fourth of July toasts in two papers name the men who died.
for_user_decision.The National Intelligencer on the seamen: Names the four men taken from the Chesapeake and describes their birthplaces and looks.
for_user_decision.General Wilkinson's speech in the court: About his arrest of Dr. Bollman, held without trial.
for_user_decision.Names in admitted stories, outside the e: The Burr documents name people arrested on suspicion; the House committee's report names the seamen; two Charleston reports name John Pierce, killed by a shot from the Leander. The excerpts end before these names.

data_issues.Herald of the United States, 4 July 1807: The RevX transcriptions of this issue are shifted by one page against the scans (RevX page 1 is scan page 2). The Chesapeake account is on scan page 2; its observation uses page 2 and the CA transcription. No other page in this ledger is shifted.
